items.reference: Okay. If I could have everyone's attention. We need to get started. We have quite a few guests here today, as you can tell, including a film crew. This is something we've never had before in the history of South Valley District. As far as I know. We're going to start with a training in a minute, but Tricia, feel free to sit down. Okay. Thank you, I will. I don't want to have you stand there. We'll turn it over to you in just a couple of minutes. Perfect. Tricia's here. She's part of Terry's team training today. I'll let Terry introduce her when we get to that point. But before we start, I wanted to have Michelle kind of explain what's going on and why we have a film crew here today. Well, first of all, thank you very much for accommodating us and letting us crash your meeting. We are here doing a project with the National Consortium of Interpreter Education Training Centers. And we received grant funding to do specific filming for vocational rehabilitation interpreting. Which is a great opportunity. There's been 3 states selected, and Minnesota, ourselves, and Boston. So, we're fortunate to be a part of this project. And what we're doing is we're taking a lot of different examples about what happens in vocational rehabilitation. So, staff meetings, such as this today, and we just had this date for filming, so that's why you're lucky to have us here today. Because you have a meeting today, and we thought, "Great." We wanted authentic stuff. So, this is a real deal meeting and we just wanted to get what we really do. We've done one on one appointments. We've done stuff with job coaches. Choose to Work trainers, We have some stuff with voc eval this afternoon. And so forth. So, we have a lot of good samples. And what's going to be happening is they'll take the footage that we have and they'll make a DVD set that will go out nationally to interpreter education - for educational purposes for VR interpreting. Because it's kind of a specialized field. As you know, the work that you do is very unique so the interpreting of the work that you do is also very unique. So, again, we appreciate your accommodating us and we're just going to be here for Tricia's presentation and then we will quickly get our stuff and be leaving.  So... 51 00:02:16,160 --> 00:02:14,160 We have some releases of information or release forms. If you happen to be on camera. We're not going to be scanning the room. Doug is there. He's not going to be scanning the room, but if you happen to be on camera, or something like that, we might send a release form to you to have you sign so we have that back just for our documentation purposes. So, thanks, Kim, we appreciate your letting us come again. Sure. Thanks for being here. So, now you know what's going on. So, you probably won't be on film, but if you want to, you can always try to get on camera. Before we start, I want to make sure that we don't forget to do our customer service award. We do this once a month. And people can nominate each other for good customer service. And then the winner gets prime parking out front. So, Kyle, would you do the honors? You usually do when you're here. Do you want me to read it, too? Sure. Tom Smith. Seeing a client with minimal notice to expedite services in the best interest of the client. Great. Nice job. Welcome back, by the way. Thank you. He's a newly married man. And he's got a good parking spot as well. Alright. I'm going to turn the time over to Terry's team now. First of all, Jeff has not been able to dial in. I can try to see if I can get him. And he was going to do the introduction, but I have it here, since I gave it to him. So, I'm going to introduce Tricia. She will give a short presentation. We'll have some question and answering session, and Tom's going to guide that. Fernando will talk a little bit about his role - he's our liaison for DSPD. And then I'll just do a closure at the end of that. So, we welcome Tricia. We're very glad to have her here. Tricia has worked for the Division of Services for People with Disabilities for nearly 12 years. She has been funded through the medicaid infrastructure grant since 2008. And has had the opportunity to research what is happening nationally for people who experience the most significant disabilities. Tricia is the administrator for the House bill 45 Support Work Independence program with DSPD and is representing in Employment First Priority legislation. Which identifies DSPD, VR, DWS to prioritize employment for people with disabilities within service delivery. Outside of work, she does have a life outside of work - True. she enjoys cooking, reading, and spending time with her family, including three crazy dogs. So, welcome Tricia. Thank you. Now that I'm sitting, I don't want to stand up. Um, is that okay? Alright. Thank you for the introduction. Again, I'm going to talk quickly about the House Bill 45 program, Support Work Independence. Kyle is my counterpart on top of all the other things that he does with VR, so - I happily tend to make the copies and get stuff ready, because the fact that he's here sometimes is a miracle. In my mind, because of how busy he is. I decided not to put the PowerPoint up so you can just have all of the slides that I'm going to talk about in your packet. And while you're opening your packet, you have several handouts that you can refer to later. You've got the PowerPoint and then you've also got the flyer, the little colorful flyer. That's something that we are distributing to potential participants, so, they're getting sent that letter. I'm going to agency fairs and using this flyer, So it's kind of a real quick introduction to what the program is. You then have a copy of all of the paperwork we use for the project. You also have a copy of the tax credit that's specific to DSPD clients. And then you also have a quick intake and eligibility checklist kind of a thing, and that's a real quick eligibility kind of reference sheet for people - for DSPD. So, if you have clients that you think might be eligible, this could give you kind of a reference to see in terms of their eligibility or diagnosis. Feel free to copy it. Feel free to use it. And we'll kind of talk about how you can check to see if someone is on the DSPD waiting list a little later. So, if you have any questions about the stuff in your packet, let me know. Really, the objective of this program is overall to develop collaborative working relationships. And I think in a lot of ways, we've done that. I probably instant message Fernando on a daily basis for one reason or another. And he's always really quick to respond. Or Laura or whomever. So, hopefully, you understanding more about this program, too, we can have even more collaboration. And the other goal is really to provide seamless support for employment. So, having that transition perfectly from Voc Rehab to DSPD without any interruption in that person's support needs. We also want to talk about just the different roles that people have in this program. That includes the community service brokers, my role as the program administrator. You guys know your role as counselors. And then the supportive employment providers, so those last two, we're going to quickly touch on because you know your roles really well. I'm just hoping that you'll have a greater understanding of what the service brokers are doing, why they're calling and bugging you. Sometimes why they may demand information that isn't necessarily appropriate. That's happened. So, just to give you a kind of awareness about what's going on with the program. We have a couple layers as all committees and things do. We have an executive management team which consists of representatives from Voc Rehab and DSPD as well as stakeholders. So, we have some provider representatives, We have legislative coalition for people with disabilities. It's a pretty big group. That gets together and we kind of talk about what's going on with the program, numbers, challenges, solutions, things like that. So, here's a list of everybody that's on that team. The executive management team. And additionally, we have our data people, so, Stacy Cummings for VR, and Tyler Black is our data guy with DSPD. And then Jolene Wyler, with the Benefits Planning program is, you guys all know, so important, is also on this committee. So, she kind of brings issues around benefits planning. We've done some data matches with her for people who are in the project to see if they've had benefits planning. That sort of thing. So, we're really trying to make sure we cover all of the facets that would affect a person's life. I then have the list of the committee members, so Fernando represents your area here in the South Valley District. And then you can see who are the other district representatives. So, I won't really touch on that one. Have you guys heard about House bill 45 before? I know several of you have been involved in it in the past. Originally, it was House bill 31 when it was a pilot project. And that was in 2006. And then in 2008, it became a long term program with a 5 year sunset and that was named House bill 45. And they we came up with the "swee" or S-W-I. I don't like to call it "swee." But the SWI program - Support Work Independence. So, that's typically how I'll refer to it as House bill 45 slash SWI or the other way around. So, that was in 2008. Sadly, in 2009, we, DSPD, lost all of their general state funding for programs because of legislative cuts. And so we discontinued that in like December of 2009 actually. And so, I think we had like 130 people that were employed. We were supporting and we had to drop the funding. It was horrible. Really, really horrible. In 2011, Representative - so, I guess the session for 2010, but for Fiscal Year 2011, Representative Menlove was able to get $150,000 of one time money in the DSPD budget and so that was this last year. And I think it was kind of tough. People got attached that one time money, knowing what had happened before. And you know just how much it takes to get a program going again. So, I think we finished the year with about 70 participation agreements. The goal was being 100. Not all of those people were employed obviously. But I think inside of all of those things, we did okay last year. So, now with this new year, 2012, she added an additional $100,000. So, we have $250,000 total to fund more people on the waiting list. And then she wrote the Employment First priority bill to actually protect the House bill 45 money. So, she wrote a bill to protect money for a bill. Does that make sense? And it's actually much more than that. So, the money's protected, so we know that it's going to be long-term. And so, I'm already getting lots of calls and people are kind of catching on that, "Oh, this is something that I want to participate in." So, that's really, really exciting. And so, what this means for you as VR counselors is you get to spend your supported employment budget. I don't know specifically what that titled money is called. It's 72 or 71. Seventy one. Okay. Originally, that was the real focus of this project was for VR to be able to spend this money. Because, I guess, historically, we spent a lot - turning money back, so, I guess now it's kind of one of those situations where we want you to spend it, right? And I'm like the only person in DSPD that has money we want to spend, too. So, it's kind of a little miracle situation going on, I think. So, what we've done this year is, um, last year, we kind of had people in the regions overseeing the program. It just wasn't working. We've taken huge cuts within staff at DSPD. And so, it's now all centralized. I do all of it. I do the referrals. I do the sending out the letters. I'm managing all of the stuff. So, if you have any questions, it comes through me. All the paperwork's coming to me. I know that sounds - arrogant maybe isn't the right word. It makes me kind of anxious every time I say it. But capacity wise, it was really the only choice that we had. so, what we have done is we use the community service brokers and that's a service that we pay for - DSPD pays for - out of this house bill money to provide some case management in addition to going out, meeting with the person, explaining the program, getting the paperwork back to me, so that I can then let VR counselors know that this person is participating. So, they are kind of serving as a bigger role now which is maybe why some of you have been getting some odd calls and you're not sure why they want all this information. It's because I am needing them to do some of that stuff for me so that I can administer the program statewide. So, with that $250,000, you know, the average is still around $1500 per person. and that includes the community service broker piece. So, probably, that's going to go up a little bit but we're just basing it on a case-by-case basis. We've spent a lot more on some folks. We've spent less on some folks. It really just depends. And that's the beauty of this program is that we have some flexibility with that within reason. I mean, obviously, if somebody is never going to be able to achieve a level of independence, we'll need to look at whether they're appropriate for this program or not because of the limited amount of funds. But we do have some flexibility within that. So, the role of the implementation team, so Fernando and his counterparts in the other offices, is to coordinate with management, with supervisors, be a technical assistance resource, so if you have questions about the case or what do you do with that Form 58? Does it have to be green or not? That question came up a while ago. It does NOT have to be green. P.S. I miss that color green. I know. Again, that was a budget cut thing. It was like, "Really? We have to buy that special paper?" Anyway, so the form does not have to be green. And so, he's really here just to help you answer questions, and be a resource. I've had him be a resource if somebody is being referred to the program and they haven't been to Voc Rehab yet, I'll kind of list his information as the contact person. So, he can kind of help them navigate through the best way. That kind of a thing. and then I've kind of listed the kinds of things I'm responsible for as the program administrator. I'm sending letters to participants. On a quarterly basis, hopefully, we are going to be doing data matches, so, looking at VR caseloads and DSPD waiting lists and matching those and making sure we're reaching people 'cause you don't always know if somebody's on the waiting list. When people are on that waiting list, they're not typically saying, "Hey, I'm on the DSPD waiting list" because it doesn't mean a lot to them. They just know they're sitting there. So, it's a way for us to identify people who may not be aware of the program. So, we're going to be doing another one of those soon. And so I send those letters out as soon as we get that information back, they send it back to me saying whether they want to participate or not, and then a referral is generated. And then as soon as I get back that participation work- participation paperwork - I then send you, the counselor, Form 58. So, that let's you know this person's going to participate. They've committed. They've signed the agreement. That sort of a thing. I've been sending all of the paperwork with that Form 58, so you have their agreement and all that kind of stuff. So, the role of the community service brokers. I talked a little a bit about that they're doing somewhat of a case management piece. So, initially, they get this referral about this person. They get their name, their address, basic information about their disability, who their VR counselor is, if I know if they're working with a CRP, a rehab provider. That information's included. They go out. They explain the program. They're also supposed to look at resources that could be helpful for them. If they haven't signed up for Medicaid, if they are having issues with their social security, getting them to a benefits planner. So, they're not just going out to fill out the paperwork, they should be able to help with some resources and supports that could be a barrier to someone's employment. Helping them to fill out ePass applications. Things like that. So, they can be a resource to you as counselors, as well. So, if you're paying a job coach, or you're paying additional money for these kinds of things, this is something that could benefit somebody who's in this program.
